meta.description: Not Confucius. The line descends from a Japanese proverb about curses recorded in 1876; the "revenge" wording and Confucius label came much later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Before you embark on a journey of revenge, dig two graves'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Confucius. It traces to an 1876 Japanese proverb about curses; the revenge wording (1915) and Confucius attribution were later inventions.

answer.label: Not Confucius — a Japanese proverb first recorded by William Elliot Griffis
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented 1876 · recorded by an American orientalist, not by Confucius
answer.sourceLine: There is no trace of this line in Confucius. Its oldest known ancestor is a Japanese proverb printed in William Elliot Griffis’s The Mikado’s Empire (1876) — “If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves” — which only later mutated into a “revenge” line and was mis-relabeled Chinese, then Confucian.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A Japanese proverb about curses, not revenge

source.excerpt: If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves.
trail: 1876: William Elliot Griffis prints the Japanese proverb “If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves” in The Mikado’s Empire.
1915: the wording shifts from “curse” to “revenge” — Griffis is credited with “If you would revenge yourself, dig two graves,” per Quote Investigator.
1951 – 1968: the saying is re-labeled a “Chinese proverb,” and Walter Winchell calls it Chinese in 1968, according to the same chronology.
Modern era: the polished “Before you embark on a journey of revenge…” line is pinned on Confucius, though researchers find no such words in his writings.
source.cutTag: ↑ the 1876 original is about curses — “revenge” was swapped in decades later
source.excerptNote: Griffis glossed the proverb as “Curses, like young chickens, always come home to roost.” By 1915 the line was being restated as “If you would revenge yourself, dig two graves,” and only after mid-century did writers relabel it a “Chinese” proverb and, later still, credit Confucius.

author.name: William Elliot Griffis
author.heading: About William Elliot Griffis
author.bio: William Elliot Griffis was an American minister, lecturer and prolific writer who taught in Japan in the early 1870s and became a leading Western authority on the country. His 1876 book The Mikado’s Empire collected Japanese history and folklore for English readers — including the “two graves” proverb that, generations later and heavily reworded, would be misattributed to Confucius. Griffis recorded the saying; he did not coin the revenge version, and neither did the Chinese sage.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: The elegant modern wording is almost universally credited to Confucius. It is not his — and it wasn’t even about revenge to begin with.

items.why: Researchers have found no instance of this saying anywhere in the writings of Confucius; The World of Chinese lists it among sayings the sage “didn’t actually say,” and Quote Investigator traces the line to a Japanese proverb instead.
The “Chinese” label only appears from the 1950s — a 1951 newspaper and Walter Winchell in 1968 call it Chinese — long after its documented Japanese origin.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest known form is a Japanese proverb about curses, printed by W. E. Griffis in 1876 as “If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves” — per Quote Investigator’s chronology.

context.heading: How a proverb about curses became a Confucius quote
lead: The saying most people know — grave, symmetrical, faintly Eastern — is a textbook example of a proverb drifting across cultures and picking up a prestigious name along the way. Its earliest recorded ancestor isn’t about revenge at all: it warns that cursing someone may doom you too, “curses, like young chickens,” coming home to roost.

Only over the twentieth century did “curse” harden into “revenge,” the origin migrate from Japan to China, and the author blank get filled in with the most famous Chinese name available. The polish is real; the attribution is not.
context.pull: It started as a warning about curses — not revenge — and it was Japanese, not Confucian.
